extracted.intended_audience: utilities, new and existing attachers, contractors, and legal counsel handling pole-attachment disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and procedures governing pole attachment applications, make-ready work, contractor qualifications, dispute resolution (including RBAT and Accelerated Docket criteria), overlashing, and EAJA award procedures before the FCC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application review timelines and denial requirements for one-touch make-ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilities must grant or deny an application requesting one-touch make-ready and respond to the new attacher either granting or denying an application within 15 days of the utility's receipt of a complete application (or within 30 days for Mid-Sized Orders or 45 days for Large Orders). If the utility denies the application on its merits, then its decision shall be specific, shall include all relevant evidence and information supporting its decision, and shall explain how such evidence and information relate to a denial of access for reasons of lack of capacity, safety, reliability, or engineering standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denials must be specific and evidentiary, tying the evidence to the statutory/technical basis for denial (capacity, safety, reliability, engineering). Timeliness is strict and scaled by order size (15/30/45 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility objection to contractor's 'simple' make-ready designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the applicable application review period (15 days, or 30 days for larger orders), a utility may object to the designation by the new attacher's contractor that certain make-ready is simple. If the utility objects, the make-ready is deemed complex. The utility's objection is final and determinative so long as it is specific and in writing, includes all relevant evidence and information supporting its decision, made in good faith, and explains how such evidence and information relate to a determination that the make-ready is not simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections must be written, specific, evidentiary, and made in good faith. If these conditions are met the utility's determination that make-ready is complex is final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys: new attacher responsibilities and field inspection notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The new attacher is responsible for all surveys required as part of the one-touch make-ready process and shall use a contractor as specified in § 1.1412(b). The new attacher shall permit the utility and any existing attachers on the affected poles to be present for any field inspection and shall use commercially reasonable efforts to provide the utility and affected existing attachers with advance notice of not less than 3 business days of a field inspection, providing the date, time, location, and contractor name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New attacher must arrange and fund surveys, use an appropriately qualified contractor, and provide at least 3 business days' advance notice with specific logistical information; allow presence of utility/existing attachers at inspections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-ready notice content and immediate damage/outage notification
rubrics_metrics.description: If the new attacher's attachment application is approved and it has provided 15 days prior written notice of the make-ready, the new attacher may proceed using a contractor per the simple make-ready rules. The prior written notice shall include the date and time of the make-ready, a description of the work involved, the name of the contractor, and provide the affected utility and existing attachers a reasonable opportunity to be present. The new attacher shall notify an affected utility or existing attacher immediately if make-ready damages equipment or causes an outage reasonably likely to interrupt service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior notice must be substantive (date/time, work description, contractor). Immediate notification obligation on damage/outage triggers remedial options: utility may repair and bill, or require new attacher to fix immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Halt and escalation when make-ready initially classified as simple becomes complex
rubrics_metrics.description: In performing make-ready, if the new attacher or the utility determines that make-ready classified as simple is complex, then that specific make-ready must be halted and the determining party must provide immediate notice to the other party of its determination and the impacted poles. The affected make-ready shall then be governed by paragraphs (d) through (i) of this section and the utility shall provide the notice required by paragraph (e) as soon as reasonably practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work must stop upon a valid reclassification to complex and the parties must follow the formal (complex) procedures and notices; immediate and pole-specific notice is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-make-ready inspection and damage-reporting timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: A new attacher shall notify the affected utility and existing attachers within 15 days after completion of make-ready on a particular pole. The notice shall provide the affected utility and existing attachers at least 90 days from receipt in which to inspect the make-ready. The affected utility and existing attachers have 14 days after completion of their inspection to notify the new attacher of any damage or code violations; if notified, they must provide adequate documentation. The utility or existing attacher may either complete remedial work and bill the new attacher or require the new attacher to fix the damage within 14 days following notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timelines: 15-day post-completion notice by new attacher; 90-day inspection window for utilities; 14-day window after inspection to report damages; 14-day cure/remedy period after notification. Documentation of damage/code violations is required for claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility-maintained lists of authorized contractors for complex/self-help and above-communications-space work
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility shall make available and keep up-to-date a reasonably sufficient list of contractors it authorizes to perform self-help surveys and make-ready that is complex and self-help surveys and make-ready that is above the communications space on its poles. The new attacher must use a contractor from this list to perform self-help work that is complex or above the communications space. New and existing attachers may request the addition to the list of any contractor that meets the minimum qualifications and the utility may not unreasonably withhold its consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilities are required to maintain lists for complex/above-communications-space work; new attachers are bound to use listed contractors for that category; requests for additions cannot be unreasonably denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor-list rule for simple work and alternative when no list is provided
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility may, but is not required to, keep up-to-date a reasonably sufficient list of contractors it authorizes to perform surveys, estimates, and simple make-ready. If a utility provides such a list, the new attacher must choose a contractor from the list. If the utility does not provide a list or no utility-approved contractor is available within a reasonable time period, the new attacher may choose its own qualified contractor that meets the requirements in paragraph (c). When choosing a contractor not on the utility list, the new attacher must certify to the utility that its contractor meets the minimum qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For simple work, utilities may impose a list-based choice if they maintain one; absent a timely available list contractor, new attachers can select and must certify qualification of their contractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility disqualification of a new-attacher-selected contractor
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility may disqualify any contractor chosen by the new attacher that is not on a utility-provided list, but such disqualification must be based on reasonable safety or reliability concerns related to the contractor's failure to meet any of the minimum qualifications or to meet the utility's publicly available and commercially reasonable safety or reliability standards. The utility must provide notice of its contractor objection within the notice periods provided by the new attacher and in its objection must identify at least one available qualified contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disqualification is limited to reasonable safety/reliability bases tied to the minimum qualifications; objections must be timely and include identification of at least one alternative qualified contractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor minimum qualification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractors on a utility-provided list, and contractors selected by new attachers when applicable, must meet the following minimum requirements: (1) agree to follow published safety and operational guidelines of the utility, or NESC if unavailable; (2) acknowledge ability to read and follow licensed-engineered pole designs if required; (3) agree to follow all local, state, and federal laws and regulations including OSHA Qualified and Competent Persons requirements; (4) agree to meet or exceed any uniformly applied and reasonable safety and reliability thresholds set by the utility; and (5) be adequately insured or establish an adequate performance bond for the make-ready it will perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All five qualifications are required; insurance or performance bond must cover work on existing attachers' facilities as well. Certification or documentation of meeting these items will be required per notice rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric utility consulting representative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The consulting representative of an electric utility may make final determinations, on a nondiscriminatory basis, where there is insufficient capacity and for reasons of safety, reliability, and generally applicable engineering purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric utilities' consulting reps have final decision authority for capacity/safety/reliability/engineering matters, but must act nondiscriminatorily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility response obligation to requests to add contractors
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilities must respond to an attacher's request to add contractors to their lists of authorized contractors within 30 days. The response must state whether the contractor meets the requirements and will be added following successful completion of any reasonable steps to begin work. If denied, the response must describe the bases for rejection, be nondiscriminatory, and be based on a fair application of commercially reasonable requirements related to safety or reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 30-day deadline; responses must be substantive and nondiscriminatory. Failure to respond in 30 days results in deemed approval (see next item).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deemed approval if utility fails to respond within 30 days and disqualification process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a utility fails to provide the required response within 30 days, the contractor proposed by the attacher will be deemed approved to perform self-help work consistent with the rules and must be added to the utility's list following successful completion of reasonable steps to begin work. A utility may later disqualify a contractor approved or deemed approved based on reasonable safety or reliability concerns related to failing to meet minimum qualifications or utility standards, but written notice must state the specific safety and reliability bases for the disqualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-response triggers automatic approval; subsequent disqualification is permitted only for specific, documented safety/reliability reasons and must be in writing with stated bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint procedures and rate-presumption for incumbent local exchange carriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints by incumbent local exchange carriers alleging denial of access to poles, ducts, conduits, or rights-of-way or that a utility's rate, term, or condition is not just and reasonable shall follow the same complaint procedures specified for other pole attachment complaints. In complaint proceedings challenging rates, terms, and conditions for contracts entered into or renewed after the effective date, there is a presumption that an incumbent local exchange carrier is similarly situated to a telecommunications carrier or cable system for obtaining comparable rates, and may be charged no higher than the rate determined in accordance with § 1.1406(d)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory presumption benefits incumbents in post-effective-date contracts but is rebuttable by clear and convincing evidence that the incumbent receives material advantages under its agreement relative to other attachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review period for pole access complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in extraordinary circumstances, final action on a complaint where a cable operator or provider claims it has been denied access should be expected no later than 180 days from the date the complaint is filed. The Enforcement Bureau may pause the 180-day review period when delays are caused by actions outside its control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected adjudication timeline is 180 days for pole access complaints, subject to pause for external delays; other pole attachment complaints follow § 1.740.

rubrics_metrics.name: RBAT establishment, purpose, and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A Rapid Broadband Assessment Team (RBAT) comprised of staff from the Enforcement Bureau and Wireline Competition Bureau shall be established to prioritize and expedite resolution of pole attachment disputes alleged to impede or delay broadband deployment. The RBAT shall gather and promptly review pertinent information, decide the most appropriate resolution process (including recommending RBAT-supervised mediation, use of the Accelerated Docket, or other action), and may require pre-filing settlement negotiations or mediation as a condition for Accelerated Docket placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RBAT has discretion to choose processes, may waive certain § 1.737 procedures in the RBAT context, and will schedule meetings and request documentation as needed; RBAT-supervised mediation is generally voluntary but can be required in specific circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: RBAT/Accelerated Docket inclusion factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether to accept a complaint or portion of a complaint on the Accelerated Docket, the RBAT shall base its decision on a totality of the following factors: (1) whether the prospective complainant states a claim within the Commission's jurisdiction; (2) whether expedited resolution appears likely to advance broadband deployment, especially in un/underserved areas; (3) whether parties have exhausted reasonable settlement opportunities during staff-supervised mediation; (4) number and complexity of issues; (5) whether the dispute raises new or novel issues; (6) likely need for and complexity of discovery; (7) likely need for expert testimony; (8) ability of parties to stipulate to facts; (9) whether parties have assembled relevant evidence; (10) willingness of complainant to seek ruling on subset of claims; and (11) other factors RBAT deems appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RBAT uses a totality-of-factors test—no single factor is dispositive. Emphasis is on whether expedited review will advance broadband deployment and on procedural/technical complexity and readiness (evidence assembled, discovery/expert needs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlashing: prior approval and permission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility shall not require prior approval for an existing attacher that overlashes its existing wires on a pole, or for third-party overlashing of an existing attachment conducted with the permission of an existing attacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlashing by the attachment owner or with owner permission does not require prior utility approval; this limits utility gatekeeping for overlashing activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlashing and preexisting violations
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility may not prevent an attacher from overlashing because another existing attacher has not fixed a preexisting violation. A utility may not require an existing attacher that overlashes its existing wires on a pole to fix preexisting violations caused by another existing attacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlashing cannot be blocked or conditioned on unrelated third-party violations; responsibility for preexisting violations remains with the party that caused them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlashing advance notice and review limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility may require no more than 15 days' advance notice of planned overlashing. The utility must provide existing attachers with advance written notice of the notice requirement or include it in the attachment agreement. If, after receiving advance notice, the utility determines an overlash would create capacity, safety, reliability, or engineering issues, it must provide specific documentation within the 15-day period and the party seeking to overlash must address identified issues before continuing. A utility may not charge a fee for review of the proposed overlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice period is capped at 15 days; utility obligations include timely, documented identification of issues and cannot charge review fees. The overlashing party must modify proposal or explain why modification is unnecessary if issues are raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlashers' responsibility for equipment and repairs
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that engages in overlashing is responsible for its own equipment and shall ensure compliance with reasonable safety, reliability, and engineering practices. If damage to a pole or other existing attachment results from overlashing or overlashing work causes safety or engineering standard violations, then the overlashing party is responsible at its expense for any necessary repairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlashers carry indemnity/repair responsibility for damage caused by overlashing and must follow reasonable technical and safety practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlashing post-completion notice and inspection timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: An overlashing party shall notify the affected utility within 15 days of completion of the overlash on a particular pole and provide the affected utility at least 90 days from receipt in which to inspect the overlash. The utility has 14 days after completion of its inspection to notify the overlashing party of any damage or code violations. If damage is discovered, the utility shall inform the overlashing party and provide adequate documentation and may either complete remedial work and bill the overlashing party or require the overlashing party to fix the damage within 14 days following notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-overlashing processes mirror make-ready timelines: 15-day completion notice, 90-day inspection window, 14-day notification of damages, and 14-day cure period. Documentation of discovered damage is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: EAJA purpose and applicability in Commission adversary adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: The EAJA provides for the award of attorney's fees and other expenses to eligible individuals and entities who are parties to certain administrative adversary adjudications before the Commission. An eligible party may receive an award when it prevails over the Commission unless the Commission's position was substantially justified or special circumstances make an award unjust, or when the demand of the Commission is substantially in excess of the decision in the adjudication and is unreasonable when compared with such decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EAJA awards are contingent on prevailing and the absence of substantial justification or special circumstances. Applicability is limited to adversary adjudications (5 U.S.C. 554) and excludes proceedings where the agency may fix lawful present or future rates and routine license grants/renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: EAJA applicant eligibility criteria (net worth, employees, aggregation, affiliates)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for an award, the applicant must be a party to the adversary adjudication and meet conditions including net worth and employee thresholds: individuals with net worth ≤ $2 million; sole owners of unincorporated businesses with net worth ≤ $7 million and ≤ 500 employees; certain charitable/cooperative associations and other entities with net worth ≤ $7 million and ≤ 500 employees; aggregation rules apply to affiliates. For eligibility purposes net worth and employee counts are as of the date the proceeding was initiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must document net worth and employee counts as of proceeding start. Affiliates are aggregated unless presiding officer finds that treatment would be unjust; participation primarily on behalf of ineligible persons disqualifies the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and burden for EAJA awards
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevailing party may receive an award for fees and expenses incurred in connection with an adversary adjudication or with a significant discrete substantive portion of one. An award will be reduced or denied if the Commission's position was substantially justified in law and fact, special circumstances make an award unjust, or the prevailing party unduly protracted the adjudication. The burden of proof that an award should not be made is on the appropriate Bureau ('Bureau counsel').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards can cover whole proceedings or significant discrete parts. The government bears the burden to show substantial justification or special circumstances to avoid an award; unreasonable prolongation by the applicant can reduce/deny awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable fees, hourly caps, and reasonableness factors under EAJA
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards are based on rates customarily charged. No award for attorney or agent fees may exceed $75.00 per hour (or $125.00 per hour for adjudications commenced on or after March 29, 1996). Expert witness awards may not exceed the highest rate at which the Commission pays expert witnesses. An award may include reasonable expenses separately. In determining reasonableness of fees, the presiding officer shall consider: (1) customary fee for similar services or fully allocated cost if employee; (2) prevailing rate in the community where services are ordinarily performed; (3) time actually spent; (4) time reasonably spent given difficulty/complexity; and (5) other relevant factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict hourly caps apply (subject to later rulemaking). Reasonableness analysis is multi-factor and fact-specific; documentation of hours and prevailing rates is critical. Expert and study costs are subject to prevailing-rate limits and necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: EAJA recoverable costs for studies and timing limitation for recoverable work
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable cost of any study, analysis, engineering report, test, project or similar matter prepared on behalf of a party may be awarded to the extent the charge does not exceed the prevailing rate for similar services, and the study or other matter was necessary for preparation of the applicant's case. Fees may be awarded only for work performed after designation of a proceeding or after issuance of a show cause order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recoverable non-attorney costs must be necessary and priced at prevailing rates; timing rule restricts recoverable legal work to post-designation or post-show-cause order work.

rubrics_metrics.name: EAJA rulemaking on maximum attorney fee rates and petition process
rubrics_metrics.description: If warranted by cost-of-living increases or special circumstances, the Commission may adopt regulations providing that attorney fees may be awarded at a rate higher than $125.00 per hour in some or all covered proceedings. Any person may file a petition for rulemaking to increase the maximum rate, identifying the rate sought, types of proceedings, and full explanation why the higher rate is warranted; the Commission will respond by initiating rulemaking, denying, or taking other action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an administrative mechanism to seek higher caps; petitions should justify the increase and specify scope of proceedings affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards against other federal agencies participating in Commission proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant prevails because it prevails over another agency of the United States that participates in a proceeding before the Commission and that agency's position is not substantially justified, the award or appropriate portion shall be made against that agency. Counsel for that agency shall be treated as Bureau counsel for purposes of this subpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EAJA awards can be imposed on other agencies whose un-justified positions contributed to the need for adjudication; procedural treatment aligns their counsel with Bureau counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents and verification requirements of EAJA application
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for an award under EAJA shall identify the applicant and the proceeding; state the number of employees (unless individual); briefly describe the applicant's organization; show that the applicant has prevailed and identify the agency position alleged not substantially justified or show that the agency's demand was substantially in excess of the adjudication; state the amount of fees and expenses sought; may include other matters applicant wishes considered; and must be signed by applicant or authorized officer/attorney and accompanied by a written verification under oath or penalty of perjury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications must be complete and verified; inclusion of organizational/employee information and clear statement of grounds for award (prevailing or excessive demand) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: EAJA net worth exhibit requirements and confidentiality procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each applicant (except qualified tax-exempt organizations or cooperative associations) must provide a detailed exhibit showing net worth of the applicant and any affiliates at the time the proceeding was designated. The exhibit may be in any convenient form providing full disclosure. Ordinarily the exhibit is public, but portions may be submitted in a sealed envelope labeled 'Confidential Financial Information' with a motion explaining FOIA exemption bases and why disclosure would adversely affect the applicant. The presiding officer may require additional information to determine eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Net worth exhibits must be detailed and often public; if confidentiality is claimed, a motion with FOIA exemption analysis is required and the exhibit must still be served on Bureau counsel (but not necessarily other parties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of fees and expenses required with EAJA application
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must be accompanied by full documentation of the fees and expenses claimed, including an itemized statement for each professional firm or individual showing hours spent by each individual, description of specific services performed, the rate used, any expenses for reimbursement, the total claimed, and total amount paid or payable by the applicant or any other person/entity. The presiding officer may require vouchers, receipts, or other substantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed, itemized, and substantiated documentation is mandatory; failure to provide adequate documentation risks denial or reduction of requested amounts.
